Part 1
SetUp and conducting the cluster analysis...
We need to standardize the numericVar variables before applying K-means. (Xi- Xbar)/Sd

```{r}
#Part a

set.seed(123)
#a)
pharmaceuticals = read.csv("C:/Users/Keeli/OneDrive/Documents/Fall 2026 Textbooks/Classwork Machine Learning/Pharmaceuticals.csv")
#names(pharmaceuticals)
# head(pharmaceuticals) to check which variables are numerical
numericVar<- pharmaceuticals[, c(
  "Market_Cap", "Beta", "PE_Ratio", "ROE", "ROA",
  "Asset_Turnover", "Leverage", "Rev_Growth",
  "Net_Profit_Margin"
)]
#to standardize the variables since Market_Cap is a very large scale value compared to things like Beta and ROE. That way Market Cap can't overpower smaller scale variables.
stdPharm = scale(numericVar)
# head(stdPharm)
# dim(stdPharm)
# apply(stdPharm,2,sd) tells us sd are close to 1
#colMeans(stdPharm) checking for close to 0
# Calculate within-cluster sum of squares for k = 1 through 6
TotWSS<- numeric(6) #to store the TotWSS for each k in a vector

for (k in 1:6) { #testing one through six clusters
  model<- kmeans(
    stdPharm,
    centers = k, #how many clusters
    nstart = 100 #picks 100 random starting points and picks the best
    )

  TotWSS[k]<- model$tot.withinss #pull out the total within-cluster sum of squares
}
#names(model) #checking the output variables
#head(model)

# Display the TotWSS values
TotWSS
# Create plot to see the elbow
plot( #graph TotWSS against the number of clusters
  1:6, TotWSS,
  type = "b", #Points and lines on graph
  xlab = "K Clusters",
  ylab = "Total Within-Cluster SS",
  main = "Clusters VS Total W-C SS"
)

# Choose the final number of clusters
k_final<- 3
#To have balance between reducing the within-cluster variance but keep the groups easy to interpret

# Run the final k-means model
set.seed(123)

#Trying multiple randome starting positions and picking the best one
FINAL<- kmeans(
  stdPharm,
  centers = k_final,
  nstart = 100
)

# Display the clustering results
FINAL

#Objective is to minimize the total within-cluster sum of squares
FINAL$size #Firms in each cluster
FINAL$withinss #Within-cluster SS
FINAL$tot.withinss #Total W-C SS
# Add the cluster assignment to the original dataset
pharmaceuticals$Cluster <- factor(FINAL$cluster)

# Part d: Assign descriptive names to the three clusters
pharmaceuticals$Cluster_Name <- factor(
  pharmaceuticals$Cluster,
  levels = c(1, 2, 3),
  labels = c(
    "High Valuation and Low Profitability",
    "Large and Profitable Firms",
    "High Growth and Leverage Firms"
  )
)
#Note our large and profitable firms are like "Blue Chip" funds 

# List each firm and its cluster assignment and name (part d)
pharmaceuticals[, c("Name", "Symbol", "Cluster", "Cluster_Name")]
#pharmaceuticals$Cluster_Name
```

```{r}
#Part b
cluster_means <- aggregate(
  numericVar,
  by = list(Cluster = pharmaceuticals$Cluster),
  FUN = mean
)
#group 21 firms by assigned cluster and calculate the average for each of the 9 numericVar variables

cluster_means[, -1] <- round(cluster_means[, -1], 2)


# Display the standardized center of each cluster
# Positive values indicate above-average values for that variable compared to the market average
round(FINAL$centers, 2)#for ease
#This is a comparison of the clusters to the dataset as a whole that is centered around 0 (standardized)

#Results
#Cluster 1: High PE ratio but very low (negative) ROE, ROA, and net profit margin. These firms have high valuations in comparison to their earnings but don't have good returns.
#Cluster 2: Higher market cap, ROE, ROA, net profit margin, and a low Beta. These firms are our Blue Chip firms with stable returns and are leading the market.
#Cluster 3: High revenue growth but have lots of leverage (debt), making these firms risky.
```




```{r}
# Compare analyst recommendations across the three clusters (Part C)
# Calculate the percentage distribution within each cluster
prop.table(
  table(pharmaceuticals$Cluster, #Rows are clusters and columns are the median recommendation
  pharmaceuticals$Median_Recommendation),
  margin = 1 #Calculates percentages by row (by cluster) instead of by entire population or by columns
)
#We see caution across the board with many analysts giving hold ratings. Cluster 3 has the largest percentage of moderate sell at 33% while Clusters 1 and 2 are either at 18% or 0%. This is likely due to their comparatively higher levels of debt making them riskier investments.

prop.table(
  table(pharmaceuticals$Cluster, pharmaceuticals$Location),
  margin = 1
)
#Cluster 2 (large and profitable) seems to be very concentrated in the US (73%) with some stragglers in Switzerland and the UK.
#Cluster 1 is evenly split among 4 countries and Cluster 3 is also US dominated (67%) with the leftover in France and Ireland.
#Cluster 2 shows us our US pharmaceutical powerhouses.

prop.table(
  table(pharmaceuticals$Cluster, pharmaceuticals$Exchange),
  margin = 1
)
#Clusters 1 and 2 are fully on the NYSE, indicating very large and established firms. They can be universally traded here. Cluster 3 has more variation, with some on NASDAQ and AMEX.

```
